explanations.explanation: Loves it is, baker. Moses says to the LORD, "Surely You love the people…" (Deuteronomy 33:3). Flaming fire and holy ones in one verse, and the next thing out of his mouth is love. I think that's a pretty tender turn.
Moses doesn't say judges here. After the flaming fire in verse 2, he turns to the LORD and says, "Surely You love the people…" That's the word he picks. Big fire, then love, and that order matters.

Warns sounds like a natural pick after a blazing picture like that. But Moses says, "Surely You love the people…" (Deuteronomy 33:3). No warning in this line, just love. The fire and the love sit side by side.

Law is it, friend. Moses says each one receives His words, "the law that Moses gave us, the possession of the assembly of Jacob." (Deuteronomy 33:4). He calls it a possession, something that belongs to the whole assembly. Not a rule they're stuck with but something they own.

Vision isn't the word Moses uses. He says the words received are "the law that Moses gave us…" (Deuteronomy 33:4). The people already had that law in hand from Moses. And it's called the possession of the assembly of Jacob, which is a pretty big deal.

A dream would be gone by morning, and this wasn't that. Moses says the words are "the law that Moses gave us, the possession of the assembly of Jacob." (Deuteronomy 33:4). It was given and it was theirs to keep. Nobody had to wake up and write it down before it faded.

True, baker. Moses says, "So the LORD became King in Jeshurun when the leaders of the people gathered, when the tribes of Israel came together." (Deuteronomy 33:5). Jeshurun is a name used here for Israel. The tribes gathered, and the LORD is King over them.

This one is true, friend. Moses says, "So the LORD became King in Jeshurun when the leaders of the people gathered, when the tribes of Israel came together." (Deuteronomy 33:5). Jeshurun is a name used here for Israel. The tribes came together, and the LORD is named as their King.

Moses says the opposite, friend. His words for Reuben are, "Let Reuben live and not die, nor his men be few." (Deuteronomy 33:6). He's asking that Reuben's men not be few. It's a short blessing, but it's all about life and numbers.

False is right, baker. Moses says, "Let Reuben live and not die, nor his men be few." (Deuteronomy 33:6). He's asking that Reuben's men not be few. That's the shortest start possible for a list of blessings, and it's all about life.

True, friend. Moses says, "With his own hands he defends his cause, but may You be a help against his foes." (Deuteronomy 33:7). Judah does his part with his own hands. Moses still asks the LORD to be a help against his foes.

This one is true, baker. Moses says of Judah, "With his own hands he defends his cause, but may You be a help against his foes." (Deuteronomy 33:7). Both halves are right there in the verse. Judah defends his cause, and Moses asks the LORD to help him.
Massah and Meribah, baker. Moses says the LORD tested Levi "at Massah" and contested him "at the waters of Meribah." (Deuteronomy 33:8). Those are the two places Moses names. Good eye on the details.

Bethel and Shiloh are real places in the Bible, but Moses doesn't mention them here. In verse 8 he says the LORD tested Levi "at Massah" and contested him "at the waters of Meribah." Those are his two spots. The waters are the clue.

Gilgal and Ai don't show up in this blessing, friend. Moses says the LORD tested Levi "at Massah" and contested him "at the waters of Meribah." (Deuteronomy 33:8). Both of those come right after the word waters. Next time, let the waters point you there.

explanations.answer: He kept God's word and covenant
explanations.explanation: Right on, baker. Moses says Levi did all that "for he kept Your word and maintained Your covenant." (Deuteronomy 33:9). The text gives the reason, so we don't have to guess. Levi held on to God's word through all of it.

explanations.answer: He wanted a bigger share of land
explanations.explanation: Land isn't the reason Moses gives, friend. He says Levi disregarded his brothers and didn't know his own sons "for he kept Your word and maintained Your covenant." (Deuteronomy 33:9). The reason is right there in the verse. It's about the word and the covenant.

explanations.answer: He was angry with his brothers
explanations.explanation: The text never says Levi was angry, baker. Moses gives a different reason: "for he kept Your word and maintained Your covenant." (Deuteronomy 33:9). That's what's behind it. It was about the LORD's word and covenant.
True, friend. Moses says, "He will teach Your ordinances to Jacob and Your law to Israel…" (Deuteronomy 33:10). Levi gets a teaching job for the whole people. That's a big job.

This one is true, baker. Moses says of Levi, "He will teach Your ordinances to Jacob and Your law to Israel…" (Deuteronomy 33:10). Teaching is part of Levi's role in the blessing. Both the ordinances and the law are named.

Upon His shoulders, baker. Moses says, "God shields him all day long, and upon His shoulders he rests." (Deuteronomy 33:12). Benjamin is called the beloved of the LORD. That's a picture of resting while someone else carries the weight.

The altar shows up in Levi's blessing, but not in Benjamin's. Moses says of Benjamin, "God shields him all day long, and upon His shoulders he rests." (Deuteronomy 33:12). The resting place is the shoulders. You can't get much closer than that.

A tent is a cozy guess, friend, but Moses doesn't use it here. He says of Benjamin, "God shields him all day long, and upon His shoulders he rests." (Deuteronomy 33:12). The picture is resting upon the LORD's shoulders. I think that's even cozier than a tent.

explanations.answer: The One who dwelt in the burning bush
explanations.explanation: That's it, baker. Moses asks for "the favor of Him who dwelt in the burning bush" to rest on the head of Joseph. (Deuteronomy 33:16). Moses is asking for that favor on top of the dew, the harvest and the mountains. The blessing for Joseph has a lot of layers.

explanations.answer: The king who ruled over Egypt
explanations.explanation: No king of Egypt in this blessing, friend. Moses asks for "the favor of Him who dwelt in the burning bush" to rest on Joseph's head. (Deuteronomy 33:16). That favor is the LORD's. It's the last gift on a long list.

explanations.answer: The elders who sat at the gate
explanations.explanation: Elders at the gate don't appear in Joseph's blessing, baker. Moses asks for "the favor of Him who dwelt in the burning bush" to rest on the head of Joseph. (Deuteronomy 33:16). That's the favor he names. It's the LORD's favor, and it crowns the brow of the prince of his brothers.

Ephraim and Manasseh, baker. Moses says, "Such are the myriads of Ephraim, and such are the thousands of Manasseh." (Deuteronomy 33:17). Those are Joseph's two sons (Genesis 41:51-52). Their names close out his blessing.

Perez and Zerah are two of the sons of Judah, Jacob's son (Genesis 46:12), so they belong to a different tribe. Joseph's blessing closes with "Such are the myriads of Ephraim, and such are the thousands of Manasseh." (Deuteronomy 33:17). Those are Joseph's two sons. Easy to mix up when the names are all family.

Gershon and Kohath are sons of Levi, Jacob's son (Genesis 46:11), so they point back to Levi's blessing. Joseph's blessing ends with "Such are the myriads of Ephraim, and such are the thousands of Manasseh." (Deuteronomy 33:17). Those are the names Moses uses for Joseph. Close, baker, just the wrong tribe.

Sacrifices of righteousness, friend. Moses says, "They will call the peoples to a mountain; there they will offer sacrifices of righteousness." (Deuteronomy 33:19). They call the peoples to come, and they bring offerings that are right before the LORD. That's a tribe doing more than minding its own tents.

Gold would be shiny, baker, but Moses doesn't mention it here. He says they will call the peoples to a mountain, and "there they will offer sacrifices of righteousness." (Deuteronomy 33:19). That's the offering named. It's about what's right, not what's flashy.

Songs of victory would be a good time, friend, but the verse says something else. Moses says, "there they will offer sacrifices of righteousness." (Deuteronomy 33:19). That's what they offer on the mountain. The singing isn't part of this verse.

True, baker. Moses says, "For they will feast on the abundance of the seas and the hidden treasures of the sand." (Deuteronomy 33:19). A feast from the sea and from the sand. That's a lot of abundance.

This one is true, friend. Moses says of Zebulun and Issachar, "For they will feast on the abundance of the seas and the hidden treasures of the sand." (Deuteronomy 33:19). The seas are named right there in the verse. So are the hidden treasures of the sand.
A lion, baker. Moses says of Gad, "He lies down like a lion…" (Deuteronomy 33:20). Gad is pictured as a strong, fierce one. That's one big cat to compare a tribe to.
A bear would be a mighty pick, but Moses doesn't use it. He says, "He lies down like a lion…" (Deuteronomy 33:20). Gad is a lion in this blessing. And the lion shows up again with Dan.

A wolf doesn't appear in Gad's blessing, friend. Moses says, "He lies down like a lion…" (Deuteronomy 33:20). That's the animal he picked for Gad. Lions run through this blessing, so keep an eye out for them.

That's it, baker. Moses says Gad "administered the LORD's justice and His ordinances for Israel." (Deuteronomy 33:21). Gad came with the leaders of the people, and that's what Gad carried out. Good work on the details.

A census isn't what this verse says, friend. Moses says Gad "administered the LORD's justice and His ordinances for Israel." (Deuteronomy 33:21). That's what Gad carried out. The justice and ordinances belong to the LORD.

Moses doesn't mention the tabernacle in Gad's blessing, baker. He says Gad "administered the LORD's justice and His ordinances for Israel." (Deuteronomy 33:21). That's the work named for Gad. It came after choosing the best land and coming with the leaders.
Bashan, baker. Moses says, "Dan is a lion's cub, leaping out of Bashan." (Deuteronomy 33:22). Short blessing, big leap. That's one verse and a whole lot of motion.

Gilead is a real place in the Bible, but it's not in Dan's blessing, friend. Moses says, "Dan is a lion's cub, leaping out of Bashan." (Deuteronomy 33:22). Bashan is the place. The whole blessing is that one verse.

Lebanon doesn't appear in Dan's blessing, baker. Moses says, "Dan is a lion's cub, leaping out of Bashan." (Deuteronomy 33:22). Bashan is where the cub leaps from. It's the only place Moses names for Dan.

Close, but the places are different, friend. Moses says, "…he shall take possession of the sea and the south." (Deuteronomy 33:23). That's the sea and the south, not the mountains and the north. Naphtali is also called abounding with favor and full of the blessing of the LORD.

False is right, baker. Moses says of Naphtali, "…he shall take possession of the sea and the south." (Deuteronomy 33:23). So it's the sea and the south, not mountains and the north. Swapping two words can really change a map.

explanations.answer: To be the most blessed of sons
explanations.explanation: The most blessed of sons, baker. Moses says, "May Asher be the most blessed of sons…" (Deuteronomy 33:24). He aims high for the last tribe on the list. And he's not done yet.

explanations.answer: To rule over all the tribes
explanations.explanation: Ruling isn't what Moses asks for Asher, friend. He says, "May Asher be the most blessed of sons; may he be the most favored among his brothers…" (Deuteronomy 33:24). He's asking for blessing and favor. No crown in this one.

explanations.answer: To be the first in battle
explanations.explanation: Battle isn't in the first words of Asher's blessing, baker. Moses says, "May Asher be the most blessed of sons…" (Deuteronomy 33:24). He's asking for blessing and favor. The strength talk comes later with the gate bolts.

Enemy, baker. Moses says, "He drives out the enemy before you…" (Deuteronomy 33:27). That comes right after the eternal God is their dwelling place and the everlasting arms are underneath. Solid ground below and the enemy driven out ahead.

Darkness is a good guess, friend, but Moses doesn't say it here. He says, "He drives out the enemy before you…" (Deuteronomy 33:27). It's the enemy that gets driven out. The word darkness isn't in the verse.

Storm doesn't show up in this verse, baker. Moses says, "He drives out the enemy before you…" (Deuteronomy 33:27). The enemy is what gets driven out. The clouds are mentioned a verse earlier, where God rides them in His majesty.
Securely, friend. Moses says, "So Israel dwells securely…" (Deuteronomy 33:28). It's a land of grain and new wine, with heavens that drip dew. Safe and well fed.

Fearfully doesn't fit this verse, baker. Moses says, "So Israel dwells securely; the fountain of Jacob lives untroubled…" (Deuteronomy 33:28). Securely and untroubled are the words he uses. That's the opposite of fearful.

Briefly isn't in the verse, friend. Moses says, "So Israel dwells securely; the fountain of Jacob lives untroubled…" (Deuteronomy 33:28). Securely is the word he picks. And untroubled comes right after it.

explanations.answer: A people saved by the LORD
explanations.explanation: A people saved by the LORD, baker. Moses asks, "Blessed are you, O Israel! Who is like you, a people saved by the LORD?" (Deuteronomy 33:29). He ends the whole blessing on who saved them. That's a mighty last line.

Strong in battle isn't how Moses puts it, friend. He asks, "Who is like you, a people saved by the LORD?" (Deuteronomy 33:29). The words that follow credit the LORD as their shield and sword. The saving is what he names.

Land is part of this blessing, baker, but it's not what Moses calls Israel here. He asks, "Who is like you, a people saved by the LORD?" (Deuteronomy 33:29). Saved is the word he uses. The land talk came earlier.

True, friend. Moses says, "He is the shield that protects you, the sword in which you boast." (Deuteronomy 33:29). The LORD is both the shield and the sword. That's the whole defense and offense in one.

This one is true, baker. Moses says of the LORD, "He is the shield that protects you, the sword in which you boast." (Deuteronomy 33:29). Both words are in the verse. So the LORD is the shield and the sword.
